column110:
Abusive and inequitable property code enforcement. 

Examples:

* WOOD CHIPS AND MULCH ARE NOT LITTER 

* Using an old dining room set for outside furniture should not be a code violation. 

* And I’m sure there are many more. Update the code. 

* Even the use of the term code enforcement is a problem. This is not a proactive stance.  

* Effective communication should be required education for all code enforcement officers. Even referring to them as officers is problematic. They should actually know their jobs.  Return calls should be required. And finally when a code enforcement officer knows part of the code is ridiculous and doesn’t want to / and sometimes doesn’t give the warning… maybe that code should be reconsidered,  removed or changed to be more appropriate and fair.

column110: Dallas needs to prioritize infrastructure, economic development, and education. I worry we are losing out to the suburbs in many of these categories. The last thing we want is for the city the metro is named for to rot. There have been many mistakes made in the past in maintaining Dallas hegemony, namely allowing the cowboys to move to Arlington and the repeated loss of corporate office tenants to various suburbs. I can tell the City is trying to turn the boat around, but it’s slow. We need the downtown buildings to be full, we need to somehow make it unprofitable to let land in high density placetypes sit undeveloped (tax it. maybe even set tax based on placetype. This could address single family areas not pulling weight, I know they’re all mad their alleys aren’t getting fixed. This could help), we need a transit system that is efficient enough, extensive enough, and SAFE enough that the white collar class will choose to use it, we need quality and equitable road infrastructure in ALL areas of the city, we need quality and equitable education opportunity in ALL areas of the city, we need safety and law enforcement in ALL areas of the city. Homelessness needs to be taken care of. Many homeless are extremely mentally ill and threatening. There is no reason the average person should have to fear using transit lest a homeless person threaten them, harass them for money, urinate in front of them, or follow them off the train. All of these things have happened to me personally.

Turning off lights during 11 pm - 6 am during spring and fall migration, would also be an energy saving practice for businesses and homeowners. column110: The city’s role in gentrification.  Older neighborhoods with older and established families are being placed in major financial burden for exorbitant property tax bills - yet living in very small houses.  It’s a form of double taxation in a way - we have to pay (continually) to keep the functionality and character of our neighborhoods with our small houses.  We use less electricity but for some reason, I’m paying 5x more than what I have for the last 16 years in electric bills - like Oncor’s meter is averaging based on my zip code not usage.  The newer homes being built are causing structural issues with our homes (same week house two doors down was getting foundation dug with huge crane - neighbor next to it had an underground gas leak, and I had an under the house water leak - not coincidence).  City does nothing!  The houses are not in keeping with the neighborhood and we have to live with years of noise, broken streets, workers throwing trash in our yards, taking up street parking and worse. Our property taxes are going up (drastically) and our quality of life is going down - all on the same street.  City does nothing because you want $$, but the people building these houses are not real Dallas.  They aren’t taking care of our city - removing trees, ruining drainage and costing even more with their loads of trash.  Builders should be forced to keep trees on the property, correct drainage issues and ensure no land movement with pier and beam in older neighborhoods.  I’ve spent more maintaining drainage with new French drains, fixing water/gas lines and would like to do more to make my house look better but the city is taking those funds for taxes - of which I don’t feel reach me and those like me.  Also, while what I just wrote is my major issue, the major underlying issue is the narcissistic Mayor just wanting news on himself with changing parties and “clickbait” decision changes,which is bad for our city (he’s turning us into a hickville joke).  Shame on him.  He’s a liar, and we know this all starts from the top.I don’t believe a thing he says anymore.  What ever happened to integrity?  Being from Dallas used to mean integrity, kindness and overall community.  It was part of the DNA of Dallas.  Not anymore.

column110: Property taxes are too high. Dallas does not have an income problem, Dallas has a spending problem. Our current budget off $4.6 Billion is significantly higher than just a few short years ago. We spend way too much money on issues that are NOT government responsibilities. Examples: Over $1 Million removing statues to satisfy a vocal few when most of the city residents did not care and would rather have had the streets repaired. Funding special interest activities such as Pride parades, at the exclusion of other activities. Defunding and underfunding police when the city has a rampant crime problem. Spending tens of millions of dollars on housing programs for low income and indigent individuals when private charitable organizations can and should provide assistance more efficiently. Many of the city expenses are NOT government responsibilities. Government is responsible for the basics and we are NOT performing this well - police protection, public education (50% of our public school students are BELOW grade level in reading and math, and are NOT college, career, or military ready when they graduate!), removal of vagrancy and panhandling, litter control, and many more items. Recommend the city focus on the basics, not the peripheral non-governmental tasks.

column110:
Rapidly increasing costs are a HUGE problem. The house I bought in 2016 (but had to sell in 2021) would now cost FOUR times (400%!!!) as much in 2024. That’s insane. Add if you add in high interest rates, it means I am now COMPLETELY priced out of the market. And there are thousands and thousands of other in the same boat.
And rents are increasing rapidly, too. The rent for tiny apartment has increased almost 25% in just 2 years. In that same period, my salary has increased about 5%. I’ve been told apartment complexes use a software program called YieldStar to collude in charging high rental rates. That surely needs to be investigated. 
PLEASE make affordable housing a high priority. Builders are building, yes, but mostly for luxury markets. And some neighborhood covenants forbid building smaller houses. Can’t there be some kind of incentive to build and allow more modest homes? And I know Texas is very anti-regulations, but renters desperately need some kind of relief. Or perhaps the city could look at changing policies to allow for some creative problem solving, like allowing more ADUs or tiny houses. 
PLEASE, PLEASE do whatever you can to address this critical problem. It’s close to reaching a crisis level. If nothing is done, people will no longer be able to afford to live here, I’m close to having to move to another city myself.

column110: City Council members demanding bike lanes where people don't ride bikes.  City Council is the main issue.  These people do not act in the interest of either their city or their fiefdoms.  It is hard to see what is in their minds.   Johnson seems only to care about economic development and sports.  ED is important, but it is not the only thing.  Johnson doesn't seem to act like people live in Dallas, only businesses.  Has he gotten so much flak from regular people about not having pro sports teams that he has to go out and get them?  I love sports, but I am sick of hearing him talk about sports.  Talk about actual people, places, and things.  For someone with a history degree, he does not show much interest in the history of his own city and, importantly, how that history is managed in relation to the reputation of the city.  I am also sick of him saying "I" all the time.  He didn't do anything all alone, and if he did, then the city has an even bigger problem than it seems.  Dallas has pockets of nice, interesting, fun, and worthwhile.  Dallas also has massive redlining still (and systemic remnants), terrible roads, and a lousy track record for uniting north and south Dallas.  City Hall is so honeycombed that it is easy to see that departments don't speak to each other or have a sense of camaraderie with each other.  This lack of camaraderie shows with how departments interact.  Citizens deserve better.

The Permitting office at Jefferson (that moved to a new location but in the height of irony, had to move back to Jefferson because the people in charge of issuing permits and certificates of occupancy couldn't even do so with their own building). I've been building for 30 years solely in Dallas and my biggest dread and deterrent to building (or doing any other type of business) is dealing with the city of Dallas permit office and the over regulation of business, construction, permitting and inspections.  The City of Dallas is a big "NO" factory because that is the path of least resistance.  I’ve literally been yelled at and hung up on for asking how I could creatively satisfy the requirement of a mop sink in a restaurant while also placing in the most inconspicuous location so it doesnt take away from the aesthetic of the restaurant design.  

There is no incentive for any staff to be creative, exercise common sense and ingenuity to solve a problems or think outside the box for unique and creative projects or ideas.  Not to mention the ridiculous amount of time it takes to obtain a permit and dont get me started on trying to get a call back or response from email from anyone in any part of the City of Dallas.  I feel like I've won the lotto on the few occasions I get a reply or cooperation with a unique construction issue or simply getting specific and accurate information on how to construct something like a grease trap for a restaurant that also has its own food truck and therefore wants the construction to satisfy all codes to try run the restaurant and food truck while also parking the food truck on site so its not burdened with a monthly expense (plus the labor and gas) required to park it at a 3rd party city approved commissary.

Its gotten so bad, I no longer build and thats a loss to the city as well as its citizens because I've taken property that was generating zero tax revenue for the city (because it was owned by a church) and converted into a cul de sac ofd 13 homes that is now receiving property tax based on a cumulative value of 15 million plus, I've done this to dilapidated properties all over town but no more, its not worth the hassle and fight and then be treated like I'm a criminal by the people in charge of issuing permits has caused me to throw in the towel, life is too short for the aggravation, building is hard enough without having to pay an entity to be my adversary.

The city should outsource all plan inspections to 3rd parties (architects, plan review companies and/or insurance companies), put the responsibility on them and the builder so the city can focus solely on a streamlined, same day permitting that accounts for the "primary concerns" that are not easily reversed and let the on site inspections take care of all other building code issues.  

And by "primary concerns”, I mean simply reviewing plans to confirm the project fits under the local zoning designations (example: someone isnt trying to build a McDonalds on a R7.5 residential lot, this would take no time to confirm or deny), make sure it meets all setbacks (which will also be confirmed by the onsite inspection of the foundation in the pre-pour stage along with the required form board survey conducted by a 3rd party, framing inspection, etc, etc), height restrictions, etc, etc.  In the case of conservation districts, have a streamlined process in place (with the option to pay a 3rd party service) to quickly review a plan for compliance with the unique requirements of a given conservation district (an architect could easily sign off on this aspect and probably do a far better job than most people who could ever be hired and/or trained by the city).  

I built very complicated 3500 to 5500 SF houses back in the early 2000’s and I was able to waive plan review and get a permit within an hour+ (assuming Jefferson wasn't too backed up when I got there).  

What happened to that fast process?  

Its not realistic for city staff to thoroughly review building plans, especially ones like mine that are 50-100 pages.  Focus on the primary risks to the citizens of Dallas at large for non compliance to zoning, height restrictions and setbacks and put the risk back on the builder who must rectify anything that isn't done according to code in the field via red tag by an inspector.  

I’ve wondered if the entire process could be delegated to insurance companies where they would issue the permit along with a policy the builder would obtain that states the project was built at or above all required codes, meets all setbacks and height restrictions, etc.  This would give buyers confidence, take pressure off city staff and weed out bad builders who cant be insured.  This is admittedly a cliff notes version of how the process could be handled but one I believe has merit.

Quit taxing business property that have already paid sales tax on when it was purchased.  Its an unfair, redundant and sneaky tax which forces people to basically have to rent rapidly declining assets like a couch, phone system, etc (for example) from the city when they city already collected sales tax at the time of purchase.  The city will still get revenue from sales tax and the property tax on the land/building so quit burdening businesses with this expense & red tape that has to be managed by another (paid) city employee.  Its an unfair & redundant tax most business owners dont have time to fight because they are too busy trying to survive, pay all their bills and hopefully make a profit after everyone has been paid.

Lastly, please pass ZOACs recommendation to eliminate minimum parking requirements for commercial and other properties as outlined in their recommendations.  As a commercial property owner, I dont need to have my parking dictated as I know the risks that come with having less parking but I also know the advantages which are often ignored (like reduced heat from less concrete, more landscape in place of ugly concrete parking lots, promotion of walking/biking/ride share, etc, etc).

The reputation among most people is to avoid doing business in Dallas because the City is just too adversarial and difficult to work for and thats not good for anyone.  Sure, the huge companies can pay 3rd parties large sums of money just to help slog through the bureaucratic obstacle course but virtually all small businesses dont have this option so be better and make doing business easier with zero adversarial mindset from staff.  Businesses (especially small ones) are not the enemy, they’re your partners but if taken to the extreme conclusion and all business is driven away, there will be no jobs for those in government or business and nobody wins in that instance.
